title: Batching policy sensitivity scratchpad — tail percentile vs fairness knobs
content:
Purpose

Quick scratchpad for sensitivity runs around continuous-batching policy knobs. Goal: capture qualitative tradeoffs between maximizing GPU throughput (avg tokens/s) and minimizing tail latency (p95/p99), while testing fairness heuristics that prevent client starvation. This is intentionally a messy working doc — notes, partial outputs, and TODOs.

Background / hypothesis
- Our continuous batching scheduler currently has 3 user-facing knobs: max_batch_size, idle_timeout_ms, and fairness_weight (0 = throughput-first, 1 = strict fairness per-client).
- Hypothesis: small increases in fairness_weight improve p99 for small noisy clients but reduce overall throughput; increasing idle_timeout reduces p50/p95 but increases p99 in bursty workloads due to head-of-line accumulation.

Environment & workloads
- Hardware: 8xA100-80GB, CUDA 12.2 kernels, NCCL 2.18, Triton fork w/ local batch combiner.
- Model: open-llm/longform-13B (decoder-only), 2048 context, kv cache enabled. Baseline FP16 quantized runtime.
- Workloads:
  * steady-mix: 500 req/s, 45% small (token<=20), 40% medium (20-200), 15% long (>200). Poisson arrivals.
  * bursty-mix: baseline + 20 short bursts (2s) of 1200 req/s, mimicking traffic spikes.
  * multi-tenant: 10 tenants, skewed qps: top-2 tenants 60% of load, remaining 40% split across 8 clients.

Experiment matrix (completed runs)
- Varying max_batch_size in {8, 16, 32, 64} 
- idle_timeout_ms in {5, 15, 50} 
- fairness_weight in {0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.9}
- Each cell: 10-minute run, collect per-request latency histogram, GPU util, kernel-launch latency distribution, KV cache hit rate.

Representative results (steady-mix)
- max_batch 8, idle_timeout 5ms, fairness 0.0: avg throughput 12.6k toks/s, p50 48ms, p95 210ms, p99 520ms, GPU util 78%.
- max_batch 32, idle_timeout 15ms, fairness 0.25: throughput 22.3k toks/s, p50 72ms, p95 270ms, p99 610ms, GPU util 94%.
- max_batch 64, idle_timeout 50ms, fairness 0.9: throughput 20.1k toks/s, p50 120ms, p95 420ms, p99 980ms, GPU util 89%.

Observations (steady-mix)
- Throughput scales with max_batch_size up to ~32 for this model; 64 shows diminishing returns likely due to kernel launch concurrency and memory pressure.
- Idle timeout smaller (5ms) reduces median latency but can degrade throughput if batch sizes remain underutilized; sweet spot at ~15ms for steady-mix.
- Increasing fairness_weight lowers p99 for small-tenant requests in multi-tenant runs (see below) but increases p50 by introducing more small batches and more frequent kernel launches.

Multi-tenant (focus on fairness)
- Baseline (fairness=0.0): top tenants dominate; small clients see p99 > 1.5s during bursts.
- fairness=0.5: small-client p99 reduced by ~45%, top-tenant p99 increased by ~18%. Global p99 slightly higher but user-level fairness improved.
- fairness=0.9: strict per-client fairness causes throughput regression (-12% tokens/s) and poor GPU packing; useful as emergency mode but not default.

Burstiness & head-of-line behavior
- With idle_timeout=50ms, we observed head-of-line blocking: long requests at head of queue cause short requests arriving during the wait to be held inside the same logical batch and see large latency inflation. Trace shows multiple short requests waiting >400ms in same batch as a long token stream.
- Mitigation: enforce per-request "max-wait" where short requests can be classified as "latency-sensitive" and allowed to preempt batch composition under fairness budget. Implemented as proof-of-concept and saw p95 for short requests drop from 340ms to 120ms with small throughput loss (~3%).

Profiling snippets
- Kernel launch overhead: 99th percentile kernel launch gap ~1.2ms when batch sizes < 12 (due to work-stealing thread wakeups). Suggest batching-thread pooling to amortize.
- Allocator fragmentation: peak GPU memory spikes when switching between batch_size 32->64 runs; nvprof showed many short-lived tensor allocations. Possible leak in cached allocator path in our fork.
- CPU scheduler: significant time spent in serialization + input-copy path when fairness_weight >= 0.5; small-batch churn increases memcpy calls.

Selected raw trace excerpt (multi-tenant run, fairness=0.5, idle_timeout=15ms):
[ts=12:07:14.241] recv req client=tenant-7 tokens=18
[ts=12:07:14.243] recv req client=tenant-1 tokens=512 (long)
[ts=12:07:14.246] batch assembled size=9 (mix short+long), schedule->gpu queue
[ts=12:07:14.247] short req tenant-7 marked preemptible
[ts=12:07:14.251] short req tenant-7 moved to fast-lane exec, latency=116ms
[ts=12:07:14.870] long req tenant-1 completed, latency=623ms

Actions we tried (quick notes)
- fast-lane preemption for latency-sensitive small requests (proto): good win, needs accounting to avoid starvation of long-running high-QPS tenants.
- per-tenant token quota window (sliding) to bound batch contribution: reduces dominant-tenant takeover, but tuning window size is nontrivial.
- batching thread pool to reduce kernel-launch overhead for frequent small batches: reduces kernel-launch P99 by ~0.6ms in microbench.
- hybrid policy: dynamic max_batch_size based on arrival rate histogram (if >x req/s, raise target batch size). Works but introduces oscillations; need dampening.

Open puzzles / TODOs
- Need longer runs (1–2h) to observe allocator behavior under steady long workload and to confirm memory fragmentation hypothesis.
- Quantify impact of serializer CPU cost vs GPU benefits for fairness >= 0.5. Measure end-to-end cost per token (CPU+GPU) for each cell.
- Explore bounded preemption: allow N small requests to preempt per second to bound fairness cost.
- Experiment with a kernel fusion patch in branch pr/467 (linked) to reduce kernel-launch overhead for small batches; run comparative tests.

Notes to self / replication commands
- Run harness: ./tools/loadtest --profile=steady-mix --model=longform-13B --duration=600 --policy="bs=32,timeout=15,fw=0.25" --collect=hist,trace,gpu
- Profiling: nvprof --metrics all --output-profile=run-2025-01-10.nvvp 
- Trace collector: /opt/ri/bin/trace-collector --stream run-2025-01-10.trace

Conclusions (working)
- No single knob dominates; operational defaults should be: max_batch_size=32, idle_timeout_ms=15, fairness_weight=0.25 for general purpose workloads.
- Provide an "latency-preserving" mode that enables preemption/fast-lane for short requests and a strict fairness/emergency mode for enterprise SLAs.
- Prioritize kernel-launch amortization and allocator stability fixes before pushing fairness_weight defaults higher.

References and links
- Related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/467
- Jira: JIRA-RT-842 (batching policy experiments)
- Design notes: confluence:Batching-Design-Notes-2024

Next steps
- Run pr/467 fusion microbenchmarks, iterate memory allocator fixes, then re-run multi-tenant experiments with fairness 0.5/0.75 to get post-fix numbers.
- Draft a short internal one-pager summarizing recommended defaults and emergency modes for on-call.

-- Isabel
